title: Zoe Meziere
text:
Stylophora pistillata is currently taxonomically recognised as one nominal species, but using reduced representation sequencing data of 379 coral colonies, we discovered five genetically distinct and sympatric taxa across the Great Barrier Reef. Demographic modelling revealed that speciation events occurred with ongoing or episodic gene flow, and that these five taxa are at different stages along a continuum of genetic divergence. Significant correlations between genetic divergence and environmental variables suggest that niche partitioning may have played a role in the formation of this species complex.
Published in Evolutionary Applications

title: Zoe Meziere
section: Connectivity dynamics in co-distributed coral species
text:
Connectivity dynamics in co-distributed coral species


Connectivity is one of the most fundamental processes driving the ecology and evolution of natural populations. Here, we investigated dispersal capacities and gene flow rates in two coral species: the brooding species Stylophora pistillata and the spawning species Pocillopora verrucosa. Using fine-scale spatial information and complementary approaches rooted in population genomics, I found that reproductive modes predict dispersal variance, with meter-scale dispersal in S. pistillata and kilometer-scale dispersal in P. verrucosa, which in turn affect long-term levels of gene flow and shape genetic diversity patterns across populations.
Published in Science Advances
Read the paper →

title: Zoe Meziere
section: Coral common garden experiment during a heatwave
text:
Coral common garden experiment during a heatwave


During the 2024 summer, the Great Barrier Reef was hit by a fifth mass bleaching event, which particularly affected the Southern region. To investigate differences in heat stress responses in the Stylophora pistillata species complex during this extreme heat event, I set up a 3-month-long common garden at Heron Island Research Station. From this experiment, we could disentangle the effect of intrinsic sensitivity (i.e., the identity of the host, the symbionts and genetic adaptation) from environmental exposure on phenotypic responses.
Published in Proceedings B

title: Zoe Meziere
text:
Postdoctoral fellow · Australian Institute of Marine Science


Hi, I’m Zoe (she/her)

I and a population geneticist, currently working as a Postdoctoral fellow at the Australian Institute of Marine Science. My research combines genomic data with ecological and environmental information to learn more about the evolutionary history and adaptive potential of Great Barrier Reef corals. I’m particularly interested in using fundamental eco-evolutionary knowledge to predict the fate of climate-threatened species and populations, and to inform conservation efforts.
I grew up in the French Caribbean, where I first fell in love with tropical coral reefs. That curiosity led me to study biology in Roscoff, evolutionary biology in Europe, and then pursuing a PhD to Australia. I was privileged to have a supportive family that prioritised education, and I care about increasing diversity in science.
I am always happy to discuss potential collaborations, so please feel free to reach out if you are interested in working together!
